query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: When Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is exposed at elevated temperatures in oxidizing or reducing atmospheres, enhanced atomic mobility drives the diffusion‐controlled formation and growth of brittle Cr-rich σ phases (and/or fine nitrides) preferentially at grain boundaries. This intergranular precipitate formation depletes strengthening solutes from the matrix and weakens grain–boundary cohesion, thereby controlling the degradation rate and eventually triggering catastrophic intergranular failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐manufactured by selective laser melting, the alloy is a supersaturated FCC solid solution with a high density of dislocations and minimal secondary phase precipitation.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled thermal exposure experiments where samples are annealed at a fixed elevated temperature (e.g., ~1000 K) for an extended duration (100–200 hours) in two distinct gas environments: one with a higher oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing atmosphere) and one with a reducing atmosphere (e.g., forming gas with H2 blended with inert gas).
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures between ~950 K and 1200 K in atmospheres with controlled oxygen content (e.g., ambient air or enriched O2) versus reducing gas mixtures, for durations of 100 to 200 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of Cr-rich σ phase (and/or fine Cr-rich nitrides) at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature exposure accelerates diffusion, enabling solute redistribution that leads to the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries. In oxidizing conditions, surface reactions may further drive Cr depletion from the grain interiors and promote precipitate growth, while reducing conditions could moderate these reactions. The resulting intergranular precipitates diminish cohesive strength and provide easy pathways for crack initiation and propagation under stress, causing catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, samples exposed in an oxidizing atmosphere will show increased intergranular σ (and/or nitride) phase formation and consequent embrittlement leading to lower microhardness and earlier crack initiation, while those in a reducing atmosphere will exhibit slower precipitate growth, retaining higher grain boundary cohesion. Catastrophic failure is expected when the density and size of the intergranular precipitates reach a critical level.
generation.baseline: The as-built SLM alloy with a largely single-phase FCC microstructure and good mechanical cohesion.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to exposures at temperatures approximately between 950 K and 1200 K under controlled oxidizing or reducing gas conditions; outside these ranges (e.g., lower temperatures or vastly different gas potentials), different degradation mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of residual nitrogen (from the SLM process) and other minor elemental segregations to the precipitate formation kinetics are not fully quantified, so the exact precipitate growth rate and critical concentration threshold remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples using the same SLM process. Anneal one set at ~1000 K for 150 hours in an oxidizing environment (e.g., air with ~21% O2) and the other set under a reducing environment (e.g., a forming gas mixture with H2 diluted in Ar). After exposure, perform detailed microstructural analyses (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to quantify the presence and distribution of intergranular precipitates, and conduct mechanical tests (microhardness and fracture toughness) to assess embrittlement.
measurements: TEM/SEM imaging to measure grain boundary precipitate size and density
Fractography of failed samples to assess intergranular cracking
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reducing atmosphere samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in intergranular precipitate formation and improved mechanical cohesion (i.e., similar or worse embrittlement compared to the oxidized samples), then the hypothesis that gas-controlled α-diffusion-driven precipitation governs degradation and catastrophic failure would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Whereas up to a certain working temperature fine precipitates can play a reinforcing role, starting from a temperature of about 950 K, the σ phase tends to swell and to preferentially place itself on the grain boundaries of the alloy. This in turn can lead to a significant reduction of the mechanical and chemical properties. This is described in the following and confirmed by a mechanical characterization with microhardness and hardness measurements that correlate with the microstructural evolution that occurs during aging.
